notes: NCBI StatPearls Whipple Disease was reread on 2026-08-27 and directly supports Tropheryma whipplei, PAS-positive/acid-fast-negative organism-laden macrophages, altered macrophage function, villous dysfunction with malabsorption, and systemic manifestations including arthralgias.
NCBI differential sources were reread for celiac disease, disseminated MAC, giardiasis, and protein-losing enteropathy/intestinal lymphangiectasia mechanisms.

The current USMLE Step 1 content specifications were reread on 2026-08-27; Gastrointestinal System remains an explicit Step 1 content category and foundational science is distributed through organ-system disease processes.

blueprint.competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

claim_audit.organism: Whipple disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive bacillus.
claim_audit.pathology: Affected small bowel contains PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria; the organism is acid-fast negative.
claim_audit.malabsorption: Malabsorption results from disruption of normal villous function by infected macrophage accumulation and intestinal involvement.
claim_audit.systemic_pattern: Arthralgias commonly precede or accompany gastrointestinal symptoms and Whipple disease is systemic.
claim_audit.distractor_1: Celiac disease causes HLA-DQ2/DQ8-linked T-cell-mediated villous injury after deamidated gliadin exposure but not PAS-positive organism-laden macrophages.
claim_audit.distractor_2: MAC can fill intestinal macrophages in severe immunodeficiency, but the organisms are acid-fast; the vignette explicitly supplies a negative acid-fast stain.
claim_audit.distractor_3: Giardia attaches to proximal small-bowel mucosa and impairs brush-border/villous function but does not cause PAS-positive foamy lamina-propria macrophages.
claim_audit.distractor_4: Intestinal lymphangiectasia causes dilated lymphatics, protein loss and impaired chylomicron transport rather than organism-laden macrophages.

adversarial_second_pass.independent_reconstruction: Migratory arthralgias followed by malabsorption, weight loss, hypoalbuminemia and a duodenal biopsy packed with PAS-positive acid-fast-negative foamy macrophages points to Whipple disease. The mechanism of malabsorption is infiltration of the small-intestinal lamina propria by Tropheryma whipplei-laden macrophages with resulting villous dysfunction.
adversarial_second_pass.mac_challenge: Disseminated MAC is the strongest histologic mimic because macrophages can be packed with organisms. However MAC organisms are acid-fast and typically occur in profound cellular immunodeficiency; the acid-fast-negative Whipple phenotype plus arthralgias makes MAC noncompetitive.
adversarial_second_pass.celiac_challenge: Celiac disease can produce villous blunting and malabsorption but not the organism-filled PAS-positive macrophage pattern.
adversarial_second_pass.giardia_challenge: Giardia causes proximal small-bowel malabsorption but trophozoites adhere to mucosa rather than filling macrophages with PAS-positive bacterial material.
adversarial_second_pass.lymphangiectasia_challenge: Protein loss and hypoalbuminemia could superficially suggest intestinal lymphangiectasia, but the biopsy would show dilated lymphatics, not PAS-positive macrophages.
adversarial_second_pass.terminology_challenge: The keyed mechanism does not overstate PAS specificity; the diagnosis rests on the full clinical/histologic pattern, not PAS positivity alone.
adversarial_second_pass.cueing_check: All five options are mechanistic explanations for small-bowel malabsorption and are comparable in length and specificity.
adversarial_second_pass.unsupported_precision_check: No prevalence, fixed age, incidence, HLA frequency, PCR sensitivity, or treatment duration is required.
